name: Apple
krispNoBenefit: Apples are the biggest ethylene source in the fridge, not a victim of it — and they out-gas any sachet. Store them apart from everything else instead.
tip: Store in the crisper drawer in a plastic bag with holes for air circulation
ripeTip: A ripe apple is firm with no soft spots and has a sweet fragrance near the stem.

name: Avocado
krispPrevents: Once ripe and chilled, slows it going from ripe to overripe.
krispEvidence: Based on published data for closely related produce.
tip: Leave on the counter to ripen, then move to the refrigerator
ripeTip: Gently squeeze — a ripe avocado yields to firm pressure without being mushy. The skin darkens when ripe.

name: Banana
krispNoBenefit: Bananas belong on the counter, and a Krisp works inside the closed crisper drawer, so it can't reach them. Keep bananas away from your other produce instead. They give off ethylene too.
tip: Keep on the counter at room temperature — never refrigerate unripe bananas
ripeTip: Yellow with small brown speckles means peak sweetness. Green tips mean it needs another day or two.

name: Blueberry
krispNoBenefit: Berries barely react to ethylene. Mold is what ends them, so keep them dry and rinse just before eating.
tip: Do not wash until ready to eat — moisture promotes mold
ripeTip: Look for firm, plump berries with a uniform deep blue color and a silvery frost coating.

name: Cantaloupe
krispNoBenefit: Whole melons ripen on the counter and are too big for the drawer. Once cut, wrap it and eat it within a few days.
tip: Store whole melon on the counter until ripe
ripeTip: Ripe cantaloupe has a sweet fragrance at the stem end and yields slightly to pressure. The skin should have a golden undertone.

name: Cherry
krispNoBenefit: Tested directly: continuous ethylene had no effect on sweet cherries in cold storage.
tip: Store unwashed in a breathable bag or container
ripeTip: Firm, glossy, and deeply colored with green stems still attached.

name: Grape
krispNoBenefit: Tested directly: continuous ethylene had no effect on table grapes in cold storage.
tip: Store unwashed in their original ventilated bag or container
ripeTip: Plump, firmly attached to the stem, with a powdery bloom on the skin.

name: Kiwi
krispPrevents: Ripe kiwi turns mushy fast around ethylene. This slows the softening.
krispEvidence: Based on published data for closely related produce.
tip: Store unripe kiwi at room temperature until soft
ripeTip: A ripe kiwi yields to gentle pressure, similar to a ripe pear.

name: Lemon
krispNoBenefit: Ethylene de-greens lemons rather than spoiling them, and the baseline life is already months.
tip: Store in the refrigerator in a sealed bag to prevent drying out
ripeTip: Choose bright yellow, firm lemons that feel heavy for their size.

name: Lime
krispNoBenefit: Long baseline life and little ethylene response.
tip: Store in the refrigerator in a sealed plastic bag
ripeTip: Firm with glossy, bright green skin. Heavier limes have more juice.

name: Mango
krispNoBenefit: Mangoes ripen on the counter, and once ripe they have only a day or two. A Krisp adds little.
tip: Ripen on the counter at room temperature
ripeTip: A ripe mango gives slightly when squeezed and has a fruity aroma at the stem end. Color is not a reliable indicator.

name: Orange
krispNoBenefit: Citrus barely reacts to ethylene, so a Krisp won't change much. It keeps for weeks in the fridge anyway.
tip: Store in the refrigerator for maximum freshness
ripeTip: Choose oranges that are firm, heavy for their size, and have smooth skin.

name: Peach
krispNoBenefit: Peaches ripen on the counter, and once ripe they have only a day or two. A Krisp adds little.
tip: Ripen on the counter at room temperature, stem side down
ripeTip: A ripe peach has a sweet fragrance, yields to gentle pressure, and has creamy yellow or warm undertones (not green).

name: Pear
krispPrevents: Once ripe and chilled, slows it going soft and mealy.
krispEvidence: Our estimate from how strongly it reacts to ethylene.
tip: Pears ripen from the inside out — check the neck near the stem
ripeTip: Press gently near the stem. If it yields, it's ripe. Pears ripen from the inside out, so don't wait until they feel soft all over.

name: Pineapple
krispNoBenefit: Pineapple does not ripen further after harvest, so there is nothing for an absorber to slow down.
tip: Store whole in the refrigerator for up to 5 days
ripeTip: A ripe pineapple has a sweet fragrance at the base, golden skin, and leaves pull out easily.

name: Plum
krispNoBenefit: Tested directly: continuous ethylene had no effect on plums in cold storage.
tip: Ripen on the counter until slightly soft
ripeTip: Slightly soft to the touch with a sweet fragrance. The skin should have a powdery bloom.

name: Strawberry
krispNoBenefit: Berries barely react to ethylene. Mold is what ends them, so keep them dry and rinse just before eating.
tip: Do not wash until ready to eat — moisture causes mold
ripeTip: Bright red all the way to the stem with a sweet aroma. Avoid berries with white or green tips.

name: Tomato
krispNoBenefit: Tomatoes keep their flavor best on the counter, out of reach of a Krisp in the drawer. If you move ripe ones into the fridge to hold them a couple more days, a Krisp in that drawer helps a little.
tip: Store stem-side down on the counter at room temperature
ripeTip: Slightly soft, uniformly colored, and fragrant at the stem end.

name: Watermelon
krispNoBenefit: Whole melons are too big for the drawer. Once cut, wrap it and eat it within a few days.
tip: Store whole watermelon on the counter until cut
ripeTip: A ripe watermelon sounds hollow when tapped, has a creamy yellow ground spot, and feels heavy for its size.

name: Nectarine
krispNoBenefit: Tested directly: continuous ethylene had no effect on nectarines in cold storage.
tip: Ripen at room temperature stem-side down
ripeTip: Slightly soft along the seam with a fragrant aroma. Avoid green-tinged fruit.

name: Papaya
krispNoBenefit: Papayas ripen on the counter, and once ripe they have only a day or two. A Krisp adds little.
tip: Ripen at room temperature until skin is mostly yellow
ripeTip: Mostly yellow to orange skin that gives slightly to pressure. A slight sweet aroma at the stem.

name: Pomegranate
krispNoBenefit: Loss is water loss and husk scald, not ripening.
tip: Store whole in the refrigerator for up to 3 months
ripeTip: Heavy for its size with a deep color. The skin should be smooth and firm.

name: Asparagus
krispPrevents: Slows the spears turning tough and woody.
krispEvidence: Our estimate from how strongly it reacts to ethylene.
tip: Trim the ends and stand upright in a jar with 1 inch of water
ripeTip: Choose firm, bright green stalks with tight, compact tips.

name: Bell Pepper
krispNoBenefit: Low ethylene sensitivity — peppers soften from water loss, not from ethylene.
tip: Store whole in the crisper drawer
ripeTip: Firm with glossy, wrinkle-free skin and a fresh green stem.

name: Broccoli
krispPrevents: Keeps the florets green instead of yellowing.
krispEvidence: Based on published postharvest data for this item.
tip: Store unwashed in a loose plastic bag in the crisper
ripeTip: Tight, dark green florets with firm stems. Avoid any yellowing.

name: Brussels Sprouts
krispPrevents: Keeps the outer leaves from yellowing.
krispEvidence: Based on published data for closely related produce.
tip: Store in a breathable bag in the crisper drawer
ripeTip: Tight, compact heads that are bright green with no yellowing.

name: Cabbage
krispPrevents: Slows outer leaves yellowing and loosening from the head.
krispEvidence: Based on published postharvest data for this item.
tip: Store whole in the crisper drawer
ripeTip: Choose heads that feel heavy and compact with crisp, tightly packed leaves.

name: Carrot
krispPrevents: Stops the bitter taste carrots pick up from ethylene.
krispEvidence: Based on published data for closely related produce.
tip: Remove green tops before storing — they draw moisture
ripeTip: Firm, smooth, and bright orange. Avoid carrots that bend or have cracks.

name: Cauliflower
krispPrevents: Slows browning on the head and yellowing leaves.
krispEvidence: Based on published data for closely related produce.
tip: Store stem-side up in a loose bag in the crisper
ripeTip: Compact, creamy white heads with no dark spots. Leaves should be green and fresh.

name: Celery
krispPrevents: Helps the stalks keep their green color.
krispEvidence: Our estimate from how strongly it reacts to ethylene.
tip: Wrap in aluminum foil — this allows ethylene to escape while retaining moisture
ripeTip: Firm, crisp stalks that snap when bent. Look for bright green color and fresh leaves.

name: Corn
krispNoBenefit: Sweet corn loses its sugar to starch conversion, which is a temperature problem. Chill it fast instead.
tip: Keep in the husk until ready to cook
ripeTip: Look for bright green, tightly wrapped husks with moist silk. Kernels should be plump when peeked.

name: Cucumber
krispPrevents: Slows yellowing and soft, watery spots.
krispEvidence: Based on published data for closely related produce.
tip: Store in the warmest part of the fridge (door or front)
ripeTip: Firm, dark green, and medium-sized. Avoid soft spots or yellowing.

name: Eggplant
krispPrevents: Slows browning at the cap and softening.
krispEvidence: Our estimate from how strongly it reacts to ethylene.
tip: Store in the crisper drawer without a bag for air circulation
ripeTip: Firm with smooth, glossy, deep purple skin. Should feel heavy for its size.

name: Garlic
krispNoBenefit: Garlic is a dry pantry item at 65–70% humidity. Sprouting and damp are what get it, not ethylene.
tip: Store in a cool, dark, dry place with good ventilation
ripeTip: Firm bulbs with tight, papery skin. Avoid soft, sprouting, or shriveled cloves.

name: Green Beans
krispEvidence: Based on published postharvest data for this item.
tip: Store unwashed in a breathable bag in the crisper
ripeTip: Firm, bright green, and snap cleanly when bent. Avoid limp or spotted beans.

name: Kale
krispEvidence: Based on published data for closely related produce.
tip: Store unwashed in a plastic bag with some air
ripeTip: Dark green, firm leaves with no yellowing or wilting. Smaller leaves are more tender.

name: Lettuce
krispPrevents: Slows russet spotting, the brown specks on romaine and leaf lettuce.
krispEvidence: Based on published postharvest data for this item.
tip: Store unwashed in a bag lined with paper towels
ripeTip: Crisp, vibrant leaves with no browning or slimy spots.

name: Mushroom
krispNoBenefit: The one head-to-head trial of an ethylene absorber in mushroom packaging found no difference in shelf life.
tip: Store in a paper bag — never in plastic (traps moisture)
ripeTip: Firm, dry, and evenly colored. Avoid slimy or darkened mushrooms.

name: Onion
krispNoBenefit: Onions are a dry pantry item, and ethylene actually suppresses sprouting rather than causing it — it is sold commercially as a sprout inhibitor.
tip: Store in a cool, dark, dry, well-ventilated area
ripeTip: Firm with dry, papery outer skin and no soft spots or sprouting.

name: Peas
krispEvidence: Our estimate from how strongly it reacts to ethylene.
tip: Refrigerate immediately — peas lose sweetness fast
ripeTip: Bright green, plump pods that are firm to the touch.

name: Potato
krispNoBenefit: The research genuinely disagrees here — some studies show ethylene breaking dormancy, others show it suppressing sprouts. Cool, dark and ventilated is what matters.
tip: Store in a cool, dark, well-ventilated area (not the refrigerator)
ripeTip: Firm with no green spots, sprouts, or soft areas.

name: Spinach
krispEvidence: Based on published data for closely related produce.
tip: Store in a container lined with paper towels
ripeTip: Bright, deep green leaves that are crisp and dry with no slimy or yellow patches.

name: Sweet Potato
krispNoBenefit: A pantry item that should not be refrigerated at all.
tip: Store in a cool, dark, well-ventilated area
ripeTip: Firm with smooth, even-colored skin and no cracks or soft spots.

name: Zucchini
krispEvidence: Our estimate from how strongly it reacts to ethylene.
tip: Store in a plastic bag in the crisper drawer
ripeTip: Small to medium-sized with firm, glossy, dark green skin.

name: Herbs (Fresh)
krispNoBenefit: In a jar on the shelf, herbs are out of the Krisp's reach. Bagged in the high-humidity drawer instead, the Krisp helps keep them from yellowing.
tip: Treat tender herbs (cilantro, parsley, basil) like flowers — trim stems and place in a glass of water
ripeTip: Bright, vibrant color with a strong aroma and no wilting or dark spots.

name: Radish
krispNoBenefit: The roots are not ethylene-sensitive; the tops are. Twist the tops off and the problem goes away.
tip: Remove greens before storing — they draw moisture
ripeTip: Firm with smooth, brightly colored skin and fresh-looking greens.

name: Squash (Winter)
krispNoBenefit: Winter squash keeps for months in a cool pantry, well away from the fridge.
tip: Store in a cool, dark, dry place with good ventilation
ripeTip: Hard skin that can't be dented with a fingernail, heavy for its size, with a dry, corky stem.

name: Grapefruit
krispNoBenefit: Citrus is only moderately sensitive and keeps for weeks regardless — ethylene changes the peel colour rather than the fruit inside.
tip: Store in the refrigerator for longest freshness
ripeTip: Heavy for its size with thin, smooth skin. Color does not indicate ripeness.

name: Apricot
krispNoBenefit: Stone fruit showed no measurable response to ethylene over three to eight weeks of cold storage.
tip: Ripen at room temperature until slightly soft
ripeTip: Slightly soft to the touch with a deep golden-orange color and a sweet fragrance.

name: Honeydew
krispNoBenefit: Whole melons ripen on the counter and are too big for the drawer. Once cut, wrap it and eat it within a few days.
tip: Store whole melon on the counter until ripe
ripeTip: Slightly waxy feel, creamy yellow skin (not white), and a faint sweet smell at the blossom end.

name: Raspberry
krispNoBenefit: Grey mould, not ethylene, is what ends a raspberry.
tip: Do not wash until ready to eat — moisture causes mold rapidly
ripeTip: Plump, deeply colored, and easily pulls from the stem. Avoid berries with visible mold or juice staining the container.

name: Blackberry
krispNoBenefit: Berries fail to mould and water loss, not ethylene.
tip: Do not wash until ready to eat — moisture promotes rapid mold growth
ripeTip: Deep black color, plump, and slightly soft. Red or purple berries are underripe and will be tart.

name: Jalapeño
krispNoBenefit: Chiles respond to ethylene only mildly, and they give way to water loss and soft spots long before ripening gas becomes the problem.
tip: Store whole in a paper bag or loosely wrapped in the crisper drawer
ripeTip: Firm with smooth, glossy skin. Red jalapeños are riper and slightly sweeter than green ones.

name: Cranberry
krispNoBenefit: Low ethylene sensitivity and a long baseline life.
tip: Store in their original bag in the refrigerator
ripeTip: Firm, plump, and deep red. They should bounce when dropped — soft berries are past their prime.

name: Fig
krispNoBenefit: Low sensitivity, and figs already give off a fair amount of ethylene themselves.
tip: Store in a single layer on a paper towel-lined plate
ripeTip: Slightly soft to the touch with a sweet fragrance. The skin may have small cracks near the base when perfectly ripe.

name: Green Onion
krispEvidence: Based on published data for closely related produce.
tip: Stand upright in a jar with an inch of water and cover loosely with a bag
ripeTip: Firm white bulbs with crisp, bright green tops. Avoid any with slimy or yellowed greens.
